text: nnWNet: Rethinking the Use of Transformers in Biomedical Image Segmentation and Calling for a Unified Evaluation Benchmark
Yanfeng Zhou1 Lingrui Li² Le Lu¹ Minfeng Xu¹
1DAMO Academy, Alibaba Group

Abstract

Semantic segmentation is a crucial prerequisite in clinical applications and computer-aided diagnosis. With the development of deep neural networks, biomedical image segmentation has achieved remarkable success. Encoder-decoder architectures that integrate convolutions and transformers are gaining attention for their potential to capture both global and local features. However, current designs face the contradiction that these two features cannot be continuously transmitted. In addition, some models lack a unified and standardized evaluation benchmark, leading to significant discrepancies in the experimental setup. In this study, we review and summarize these architectures and analyze their contradictions in design. We modify UNet and propose WNet to combine transformers and convolutions, addressing the transmission issue effectively. WNet captures long-range dependencies and local details simultaneously while ensuring their continuous transmission and multi-scale fusion. We integrate WNet into the nnUNet framework for unified benchmarking. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in biomedical image segmentation. Extensive experiments demonstrate their effectiveness on four 2D datasets (DRIVE, ISIC-2017, Kvasir-SEG, and CREMI) and four 3D datasets (Parse2022, AMOS22, BTCV, and ImageCAS). The code is available at https : //github.com/Yanfeng-Zhou/nnWNet.
1. Introduction

Segmentation is a fundamental task in biomedical image analysis, where the goal is to assign a class label to each pixel (voxel). With the development of deep learning, biomedical image segmentation has achieved superior results [16, 23, 25, 33, 41, 58, 60–62]. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) based on the encoder-decoder architecture are a mainstream paradigm [25, 41]. Two key characteristics of CNNs are local connections and parameter sharing. Local connections ensure that the extracted features are specific to the local input, while parameter sharing makes the features translationally invariant. This design enhances computational efficiency while enabling CNNs to focus on local details.

Recently, the sequence-to-sequence transformer architecture has gained significant attention [11, 34, 47]. It utilizes a global self-attention mechanism to capture longrange dependencies and global information. However, it also brings the limitations of high computational overhead and a tendency to overlook local details.

Some studies have attempted to combine convolutions and transformers to leverage both local and global receptive fields simultaneously. These combination strategies include: alternately stacking convolutional layers and transformer layers [3, 14, 29], using convolution (Conv) to build the encoder and transformer (Trans) to build the decoder (or vice versa) [17, 18], and incorporating transformers into bottleneck blocks or bridge blocks between the encoder and decoder [6, 7, 48, 50]

However, these designs are contradictory and flawed. The purpose of the transformer layer is to extract long-range dependencies and generate corresponding global features, while the convolutional layer is to capture local details and generate locally-focused features. The current combination method forces the transformer layer to use local features as input to extract global features, and enforces the convolutional layer to operate on global features to extract local details. Global features and local features are generated alternately and cannot be transmitted continuously and stably throughout the model. This contradiction leads to feature confusion and instability of the training process.

In addition, the current biomedical image segmentation models lack a unified evaluation benchmark [26]. Different studies have significant discrepancies in experimental datasets, image preprocessing strategies (such as resampling, region of interest cropping), training and validation set divisions, evaluation metrics, and some key hyperparameters (such as patch size, loss function, and number of training epochs). This lack of standardization makes it challenging to compare results across studies and evaluate the true performance of different models. Some models may excel in specific datasets, but fail to generalize in others. Moreover, certain models that claim state-of-the-art performance may not perform well under a unified benchmark and even worse than a well-designed UNet.

In this study, we review various biomedical image segmentation models based on convolutions and transformers, abstracting them into several typical architectures and analyzing the contradictions and defects within these designs. To effectively incorporate transformers into the fully convolutional UNet [41] for extracting global features while addressing these issues, we propose a modified architecture, WNet. WNet captures both long-range dependencies and local details, ensuring continuous transmission of these two types of features without alternation or confusion. We then integrate WNet into the automatically configured framework, nnUNet [25], resulting in nnWNet. Extensive experiments on a unified evaluation benchmark based on the nnUNet framework demonstrate its effectiveness. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on four 2D datasets and four 3D datasets with different segmentation objects, data scales, and image modalities.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We systematically summarize and classify various biomedical image segmentation models based on convolutions and transformers, and analyze their contradictions and defects.

• We slightly adjust the UNet architecture and propose WNet. WNet focuses on both long-range dependencies and local details, ensuring continuous transmission of these two types of features without alternation or confusion throughout the network.
• We integrate WNet into the nnUNet framework, resulting in nnWNet. nnWNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on four 2D datasets and four 3D datasets within a unified evaluation benchmark.
2. Related Work

Convolution-Based Biomedical Image Segmentation. The efficient and lightweight U-shaped CNNs are dominant in biomedical image segmentation. They can retain the position information of the boundaries and alleviate overfitting under the limited data volume of biomedical images. Some studies add or improve various designs to the U-shaped CNNs to better extract features. UNet++ [62] redesigns the skip connection between the encoder and decoder to achieve multi-scale feature aggregation. Attention UNet [37] integrates the attention gate module into UNet [41] to better focus on target structures of varying shapes and sizes. [45] proposes a full convolutional U-shaped network (CMUNet) that incorporates hybrid convolution and multi-scale attention gate. Furthermore, some studies have extended these architectures to 3D to meet the needs of volumetric segmentation. [36] proposes a fully convolutional 3D network, VNet. ConResNet [55] proposes inter-slice context residual learning to improve the ability of spatial context perception. [57] proposes a low-frequency and high-frequency fusion network, XNet, for fully- and semi-supervised biomedical image segmentation.

Transformer-Based Biomedical Image Segmentation. The transformer model treats images as sequences of small patches. It employs a self-attention mechanism based on fully connected networks to capture long-range dependencies across the entire image and uses position encoding to represent the spatial relationships between the patches. Several studies have explored integrating transformers into U-shaped architectures. Common strategies include: pure transformer UNet without convolutional layers, such as SwinUNet [5], D-Former [12], nnFormer [56]; replacing the convolutional encoder or decoder with the transformer, such as TC-CoNet [8], ConvTransSeg [13], UN-ETR [18], Swin UNETR [17], 3D UX-Net [32]; incorporating transformer-based bridges or bottlenecks between the encoder and decoder, such as CoTr [50], MissFormer [24], DCA [1], TransAttUNet [6]; stacking convolutional layers and transformer layers in series or parallel, such as ConvFormer [14], H2Former [20], DuAT [46], MaxViT-UNet [29]. Furthermore, some studies are focused on optimizing the self-attention mechanism to reduce computational costs and memory consumption, such as BRAU-Net++ [30], UNETR++ [43]. However, these architectural designs have the defect of alternating and confusing transmission between global and local features. We discuss this issue in more detail in Section 3.1.

nnUNet. nnUNet [25, 26] is an automatically configured segmentation framework that sets image preprocessing, data augmentation, and training hyperparameters. It not only serves as an out-of-the-box segmentation solution but also provides a unified benchmark for evaluating model performance. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive and fair comparison based on the nnUNet framework.
3. Method

In Section 3.1, we review and summarize various encoderdecoder architectures and analyze the contradictions of current designs combining transformers and convolutions. In Section 3.2, we make slight adjustments to the fully convolutional UNet to propose WNet, which integrates transformers and addresses the contradictions. In Section 3.3, we integrate WNet into the nnUNet framework for unified benchmarking.

text: 3.1. Discussion on Encoder-Decoder Architectures

As shown in Figure 1, current encoder-decoder models can be summarized and abstracted into three main architectures: encoder-decoder, encoder-bottleneck-decoder, and encoder-bridge-decoder. These three architectures are composed of four modules: encoder, decoder, bottleneck, and bridge. These four modules can not only be the sequential connection of pure convolutional layers or pure transformer layers, but also the series or parallel connection of convolutional layers and transformer layers. Table 2 lists these architectures along with some corresponding models. Convolution focuses on capturing local details, while transformer emphasizes global relationships. Their combination has the potential to enhance the feature representation capability.

However, current combination strategies are contradictory. Whether using transformers as encoders and convolutions as decoders (or vice versa), or stacking convolutional and transformer layers alternately, they force the transformer layers to utilize local features as input to capture long-range dependencies, and force the convolutional layers to use global features as input for extracting local details. It disrupts the continuous and stable flow of global and local features throughout the model, leading to training instability and significant performance degradation. We observe this phenomenon in comparative experiments in Section 4.3.

text: 3.2. Integrating Transformers without Contradictions

To integrate the transformer into the encoder-decoder architecture, and ensure that global and local features can be continuously transmitted without interruption and confusion, we slightly adjust UNet [41] and propose WNet. Figure 2 shows an overview of WNet. WNet consists of two cascaded encoder-decoder architectures, performs Overlapped Patch Embedding (OPE) on the input images, uses the Local Scope Blocks (LSBs) to construct multi-scale encoding and decoding layers, and introduces the Global Scope Bridges (GSBs) between the encoding and decoding layers at each scale. We employ convolutional layers as LSBs to extract local details, and use transformer layers as GSBs to capture long-range dependencies. LSBs and GSBs perform feature fusion to exchange information at each encoding-decoding scale. We explain the motivation of architecture design in detail in the supplementary material.

Specifically, the overlapped feature embedding is implemented by 3×3 convolutions with a stride of 1 and down-sampling. LSBs are implemented by 3×3 residual blocks [21] with a stride of 1 and down/up-sampling. GSBs are implemented by transformers with global attention mechanism. Feature fusion is implemented by channel concatenation. We compare various attention mechanisms and fusion strategies in ablation studies in Section 4.6. Note that the local features based on LSBs contain implicitly positional relationships, and since LSBs and GSBs can exchange information, we do not introduce additional positional encoding in GSBs.

image_caption: Figure 3. Transmission of global and local features. (a) Transmission of local features. (b) Transmission of global features. The two features flow and fuse continuously without interruption.

text: How to address the contradiction? From Figure 3, we can see that the global and local features in WNet can flow continuously throughout the model and exchange informa-

tion with each other at each scale, which not only addresses the contradiction, but also effectively fuses the global and local features into a unified representation. We compare the effective receptive fields (ERFs) of LSBs and GSBs at different scales in Figure 4. The ERFs of LSBs are small, whereas the ERFs of GSBs are large, and they are complementary. This indicates that LSBs primarily capture local features, while GSBs focuse on non-local features. More details on the visualization of the ERFs can be found in the supplementary material. In addition, WNet is just an extension of the U-shaped architecture without any complex operations. It has fewer parameters than nnUNet. We compare the number of parameters and the performance of different models in Section 4.3.

text: 3.3. Calling for a Unified Evaluation Benchmark

Due to the diversity of biomedical images in terms of image sizes, dimensions, modalities, imaging regions, pixel (voxel) sizes, segmentation objects, data scales, and pathological changes, there are significant differences even among datasets for the same clinical application. It results in a lack of standardized training and validation set divisions and consistent evaluation metrics for evaluating performance. Some studies attempt to refine image preprocessing (such as image resampling and region of interest cropping) and optimize key hyperparameters (such as patch size and the number of training epochs) to ensure that their models perform better.

In general, due to the lack of a unified evaluation benchmark, comparative experiments are no longer merely a competition of model architectures. nnUNet [25, 26] is an automatically configured segmentation framework. More importantly, it provides a unified benchmark for purely and fairly comparing various architectures. We integrate WNet into the nnUNet framework to standardize the experimental setup.
4. Experiments
4.1. Datasets

We evaluate our model on four 2D datasets (DRIVE [44], ISIC-2017 [9], Kvasir-SEG [27], and CREMI [12]) and four 3D datasets (Parse2022 [35], AMOS22 [28], BTCV [31], ImageCAS [53]). Table 2 presents the details on their experimental setup. Additional information on these eight datasets is presented in the supplementary materials. From Table 2, these datasets cover different modalities, dimensions, imaging regions, data scales, and segmentation objects. Evaluating model performance is more representative and convincing.
4.2. Unified Evaluation Benchmark

We implement our model via nnUNet framework (version 2.3.1). Training and inference of all the models are performed on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. All models are trained from scratch. To balance training time and effect, we use 2d and 3d\_lowres trainer for 2D and 3D datasets, respectively. The number of training epochs is set to 200 for 2D datasets and 500 for 3D datasets. We use five-fold cross-validation to evaluate the segmentation results and use the Jaccard index (Jaccard), Dice coefficient (Dice), 95thpercentile Hausdorff distance (95HD), and average surface distance (ASD) as performance metrics. Jaccard and Dice emphasize pixel-wise accuracy, whereas 95HD and ASD emphasize boundary accuracy. Furthermore, we only use the output of models to evaluate performance without any additional post-processing. Other configurations (such as learning rate, loss function, patch size, and optimizer) are the default in the nnUNet framework.

text: 4.5. Qualitative Results

Figure 5 and Figure 6 show various qualitative results of different models. Based on the continuous flow and multiscale fusion of global and local features, nnWNet achieves better pixel-wise accuracy and contour accuracy. More qualitative results are available in the Supplemental Material.
4.6. Ablation Studies
To verify the effectiveness of each component, we perform the following ablation studies on four 2D datasets.

Comparison of Different Self-Attention. Table 5 compares the performance of adding different self-attentions to GSBs, including depth-wise convolution (DW Conv) with large kernel [32], pooling [52], and efficient multi-head selfattention (E-MHSA) [15]. Pooling achieves better results. We use pooling as self-attention to all relevant experiments in Table 3.

Comparison of Fusion Strategies. Table 6 compares different fusion strategies of global and local features. We find that the channel concatenation used by the raw UNet achieves better performance. We apply it to all relevant experiments in Table 3.

Effectiveness of Combining Convolution and Transformer. We replace LSBs with PoolFormers and GSBs with residual blocks to generate a pure transformer WNet and a pure convolutional WNet, respectively. Table 7 compares the performance of hybrid, pure convolutional, and pure transformer architectures. Overall, the hybrid architecture demonstrates superior results. Note that the pure convolutional architecture may achieve better contour accuracy because convolution focuses on local details and is sensitive to boundaries.

Necessity of Continuous Transmission of Global and Local Features. We replace the encoder and decoder in the raw UNet [41] to demonstrate the significance of continuous transmitting global and local features. Specifically, we implement pure convolution, pure transformer, series connection of convolution and transformer, and parallel connection of convolution and transformer to construct the encoder and decoder. Table 8 compares the performance of these architectures. Our findings indicate that the series connection has a negative effect. This may be due to the series connection forcing global and local features to be generated alternately, which hinders continuous transmission. In contrast, the parallel connection and fusion before each down-sampling yields positive results because it avoids the conflict of capturing long-range dependencies from local features while simultaneously extracting local details from global features. The performance of using a convolutional encoder with a transformer decoder is similar to that of using a transformer encoder with a convolutional decoder, with both architectures performing between the series and parallel connections. Furthermore, we find that the combination of transformer and convolution outperforms the pure convolutional architecture, further proving the necessity of focusing on both global and local features.

text: 5. Conclusion

We systematically summarize the transformer-based encoder-decoder architectures for biomedical image segmentation and analyze the contradictions within their designs. To incorporate the transformer and address the contradictions, we slightly adjust UNet and propose WNet.

WNet can capture long-range dependencies and local details simultaneously and ensure their continuous transmission and multi-scale fusion. We integrate WNet into the nnUNet framework for unified benchmarking. Our model achieves state-of-the-art biomedical image segmentation, and extensive experiments on four 2D datasets and four 3D datasets demonstrate its effectiveness.
